name: Carl Braden
bio: Carl Braden was a white Louisville newspaperman convicted of sedition under a Kentucky state law after he and his wife Anne bought a house and sold it to a Black family, the Wades, in an all-white neighborhood. After the home was dynamited, the state prosecuted the white buyers rather than the bombers; Braden was sentenced in 1954 to 15 years and held under a $40,000 appeal bond before being freed pending appeal on July 12, 1955.
charges: Sedition (Kentucky state sedition law) — for helping a Black family buy a home in a white neighborhood
convicted: Convicted December 1954; 15 years; freed on bond pending appeal July 1955
sentence: 15 years and a $5,000 fine; served ~8 months before bond

name: Anne Braden
bio: Anne Braden was a white civil-rights activist and journalist indicted for sedition in Louisville, Kentucky alongside her husband Carl after the couple helped a Black family, the Wades, move into a white neighborhood. Her trial was postponed pending the appeals in her husband's case and the U.S. Supreme Court's ruling on state sedition laws; she went on to a long career as a Southern civil-rights organizer.
charges: Sedition (Kentucky state sedition law) — for helping a Black family buy a home in a white neighborhood

name: Louise Gilbert
bio: Louise Gilbert was a social worker and member of the Church of the Brethren, active in interracial work, indicted for sedition in Louisville, Kentucky as one of seven white defendants charged for helping the Wade family move into a white neighborhood. Police seized her cookbook and Sunday-school magazines as 'evidence.'
charges: Sedition (Kentucky state sedition law) — in the Wade-Braden desegregation case

name: Steve Nelson
bio: Steve Nelson was a Communist leader and Spanish Civil War veteran convicted under Pennsylvania's state sedition law and sentenced to 20 years and a $10,000 fine, in addition to a federal Smith Act conviction. The Pennsylvania Supreme Court reversed the sedition conviction, and the state's appeal became the landmark 1956 case Pennsylvania v. Nelson, which held that the federal Smith Act preempted state sedition laws.
charges: Pennsylvania state sedition law; and the federal Smith Act
convicted: Convicted; state conviction reversed; before the U.S. Supreme Court in 1955
sentence: 20 years and $10,000 (state); plus a five-year Smith Act sentence

name: Thomas Quinn
bio: Thomas Quinn was a Pittsburgh organizer for the United Electrical Workers cited for contempt of Congress after refusing, on First and Fifth Amendment grounds, to answer a House Un-American Activities Committee probe of the union in 1949. His conviction was reversed by the U.S. Supreme Court in Quinn v. United States in May 1955.
charges: Contempt of Congress — for refusing to answer HUAC
convicted: Convicted; reversed by the Supreme Court (Quinn v. United States, 1955)
sentence: Six months and a $500 fine; conviction reversed

name: Phil Bart
bio: Phil Bart was a former general manager of the Daily Worker cited for contempt of Congress after refusing, on constitutional grounds, to answer a House Un-American Activities Committee's questions. His conviction was reversed by the U.S. Supreme Court in May 1955 in the same set of rulings as the Emspak and Quinn cases.
charges: Contempt of Congress — for refusing to answer HUAC
convicted: Convicted; reversed by the Supreme Court (1955)

name: Joseph Starobin
bio: Joseph Starobin was a writer and the former foreign editor of the Daily Worker who was voted a contempt-of-Congress citation by the Senate in August 1955 after refusing to disclose his party affiliations, which he called 'my private affair.' He said he was being harassed in part because he used the same publisher as the recanting informer Harvey Matusow.
charges: Contempt of Congress — for refusing to disclose party affiliations

name: Wendell Furry
bio: Wendell Furry was a Harvard University physicist cited for contempt of Congress after refusing, on constitutional grounds, to answer questions from Senator McCarthy's subcommittee about alleged Communist associations. His contempt case was pending in 1955.
charges: Contempt of Congress — for refusing to answer McCarthy's subcommittee
convicted: Cited for contempt; case pending in 1955
sentence: Faced prosecution for contempt of Congress

name: Leon J. Kamin
bio: Leon J. Kamin was a research assistant cited for contempt of Congress after refusing to answer Senator McCarthy's subcommittee; his case was among the contempt prosecutions pending in 1955. He later became a prominent psychologist and critic of IQ testing.
charges: Contempt of Congress — for refusing to answer McCarthy's subcommittee
convicted: Cited for contempt; case pending in 1955
sentence: Faced prosecution for contempt of Congress

name: Diantha Hoag
bio: Diantha Hoag was an electrical worker cited for contempt of Congress after refusing to answer Senator McCarthy's subcommittee about her associations; her contempt case was among those pending in 1955.
charges: Contempt of Congress — for refusing to answer McCarthy's subcommittee
convicted: Cited for contempt; case pending in 1955
sentence: Faced prosecution for contempt of Congress

name: William L. Patterson
bio: William L. Patterson was the Black executive secretary of the Civil Rights Congress and author of the petition 'We Charge Genocide,' jailed for contempt for refusing to produce CRC membership records demanded by the government in its drive to destroy the organization. He served three months at West Street before the U.S. Court of Appeals reversed his conviction in January 1955, holding he could not be jailed for invoking his privilege against self-incrimination.
charges: Contempt — for refusing to surrender Civil Rights Congress records
convicted: Jailed; conviction reversed by the Court of Appeals January 1955

name: Edward J. Fitzgerald
bio: Edward J. Fitzgerald was a former New Deal government official, named by the informer Elizabeth Bentley, who was prosecuted as the second test case of the 1954 Compulsory Testimony (immunity) Act after refusing to answer a federal grand jury investigating alleged wartime espionage. He was convicted of contempt in August 1955, sentenced to six months, and appealed, calling the case 'a curtain raiser for the 1956 elections.'
charges: Contempt — refusing to testify under the Compulsory Testimony (immunity) Act of 1954
convicted: Convicted of contempt August 1955; on appeal
sentence: Six months; released on bail pending appeal

name: Anna H. Morgan
bio: Anna H. Morgan — known to supporters as 'Grandmother Morgan' — was fined $3,200 (a hundred dollars on each of 32 counts) for invoking the Fifth Amendment before the Ohio Un-American Activities Commission. She appealed the fine, declaring 'I'm fighting mad.'
charges: Contempt — for invoking the Fifth Amendment before the Ohio Un-American Activities Commission

name: Willard Uphaus
bio: Dr. Willard Uphaus was the director of World Fellowship, a religious pacifist organization, targeted by New Hampshire's one-man subversion probe under Attorney General Louis Wyman for running peace seminars. He refused on First Amendment grounds to turn over the names of seminar guests; fined in 1955 and fighting the inquiry, he was later jailed for a year for contempt.
charges: Contempt — for refusing to give a state subversion probe the names of seminar attendees
convicted: Fined 1955; case on appeal (later jailed for contempt)
sentence: $500 fine; later a year in jail

name: Owen Lattimore
bio: Owen Lattimore was a Johns Hopkins scholar of Asia whom Senator McCarthy branded the 'top Soviet agent' in America. Indicted for perjury in 1952 over his testimony before the McCarran Internal Security Subcommittee, he saw the key counts repeatedly thrown out by Judge Luther Youngdahl; Attorney General Brownell finally moved to drop all charges, and the indictment was dismissed on June 30, 1955.
charges: Perjury — arising from testimony before the McCarran Internal Security Subcommittee

name: Sam Hirsch
bio: Sam Hirsch was a former director of Miami Beach's Biltmore Playhouse indicted on eight counts of perjury in 1955 for denying Communist Party membership before a grand jury in State Attorney George Brautigam's Florida red-hunt. The state's sole witness against him had a long record of drunkenness convictions.
charges: Perjury — for denying Communist Party membership before a grand jury
sentence: Faced up to 20 years per count

name: Walter Lohman
bio: Walter Lohman was a rank-and-file member of the United Electrical Workers in Dayton, Ohio, convicted in September 1955 of falsely signing a Taft-Hartley non-Communist affidavit — a prosecution brought years after the alleged offense. He remained free on bail pending appeal.
charges: Falsely signing a Taft-Hartley non-Communist affidavit

name: Harry Bridges
bio: Harry Bridges was the Australian-born president of the International Longshoremen's and Warehousemen's Union and the target of repeated government efforts to deport or denaturalize him over alleged Communist ties. In 1955 the government's fifth attempt in 21 years — a civil suit to strip his citizenship — went to trial in San Francisco and was dismissed in August by Judge Louis Goodman, who found the government's witnesses 'inherently flimsy.'
charges: Denaturalization — alleging he concealed Communist Party membership at his 1945 naturalization
